title: Recover the Alphabet Order
statement:
An invented language uses some of the lowercase letters a–z, but in its own alphabetical order, which you do not know. You get a list words that is claimed to be sorted by that order, the way a dictionary is: two words are compared at the first position where they differ, and if one word is a prefix of the other, the shorter one comes first.

Return a string that contains every letter appearing in words exactly once, in an order under which the list really is sorted. Letters the list says nothing about may go anywhere, so any valid order is accepted.

If no order can make the list sorted, return the empty string "".

examples.why: The pairs give t before r, k before t, and q before t. Nothing compares k with q, so "qktr" is accepted too. Only the first difference counts: "kr" before "tq" says k before t and nothing about r and q.
"mo" is a prefix of "mop", so it would have to come first in any order.
The pairs say x before y, y before z, and z before x. That is a loop, so no order works.

hints: Two neighbouring words tell you about one pair of letters at most: the pair at the first position where they differ. What does that pair tell you?
Each such pair is a rule "x comes before y". With letters as nodes and rules as edges, you need an order where every edge points forward: a topological order.

Build the rules from neighbouring words only, then run Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly output a letter with no remaining rule in front of it. If letters are left over, there is a loop. Also check the special case of a longer word right before its own prefix.

explain.intuition:
A sorted dictionary hides its alphabet in the first difference between neighbouring words. If "kr" comes right before "tq", then k comes before t. Nothing else can be read from that pair: after the first difference the letters are free. Comparing only neighbours is enough, because sorted order is transitive: what a pair of words further apart would tell you already follows from the neighbours in between.

Each rule "x before y" is a directed edge, so the alphabet is a topological order of the letters. Kahn's algorithm builds one: count, for each letter, how many rules point at it, start with the letters that have none, and each time you output a letter, remove its outgoing rules. If a loop exists, the letters on it never reach zero, so the output comes up short: return "". This is the same check a bundler makes when it orders modules by their imports and reports a circular dependency.

One input is broken in a way no graph shows: a word followed by its own strict prefix, like "mop" then "mo". There is no differing letter, yet no order can put the longer word first. Check for that while scanning pairs.
steps: Register every letter that appears in any word, each with an empty rule list and in-degree 0.
For each neighbouring pair, find the first position where they differ. If there is none and the first word is longer, return "". Otherwise add the rule a[j] → b[j] once.
Put every letter with in-degree 0 in a queue.
Pop a letter, append it to the answer, and lower the in-degree of each letter it points to; any that reach 0 join the queue.
If the answer holds every letter, return it; otherwise there was a loop, so return "".
pitfalls: Adding a rule for every position where two words differ instead of only the first. In example 1 that adds "r before q" and invents a loop.
Leaving out letters that never appear in a rule. Every letter in the words must be in the answer.
Missing the prefix case: ["mop", "mo"] has no differing letter but is still invalid. The reverse, ["mo", "mop"], is fine.

complexity.time: O(C), where C is the total number of characters in all words
complexity.space: O(1) beyond the input: at most 26 letters and 26² rules

solutions.title: Kahn's algorithm (BFS)
solutions.idea: Read one rule from each neighbouring pair, then output letters whose in-degree has dropped to 0. Fewer letters out than in means a loop.

solutions.title: DFS with three colours
solutions.idea: Depth-first search from each letter, writing a letter down after everything that must follow it. Meeting a letter that is still on the current path means a loop. Reverse the post-order.

followups: Return "unique" if the list pins down exactly one order. How can Kahn's algorithm tell? (Look at the queue size.)
The list is a stream of words too large to store. Can you still build the rules?
